title: High Mountain Environments: the Himalayas

walkthroughs.body_html: The Himalayas are forming as the Indian plate collides with Eurasia. Rates of uplift around 5-10 mm/yr keep peaks like Everest (8,849 m) growing while erosion races to keep pace. Steep slopes and active seismicity (Nepal earthquake 2015) define the hazardscape.

Himalayan glaciers feed the Indus, Ganges, Brahmaputra, Yangtze and Mekong rivers, supplying water to nearly 2 billion people downstream. Most glaciers have lost mass since the 1970s; black carbon and dust deposition accelerate melt. GLOFs threaten communities such as Pokhara and parts of Bhutan.

Sherpa physiology shows genetic adaptation to hypoxia (EPAS1 variants). Terraced agriculture, seasonal migration to lowlands and pastoralism shape mountain livelihoods. Tourism — climbing on Everest and Annapurna — provides income but raises environmental concerns about waste, deforestation and Sherpa safety.

mcqs.q: What is hydraulic action in a river?
options: Deltas form in cold climates and estuaries in warm climates.
Hydraulic action is when the river dissolves rocks chemically.
The force of moving water itself compressing air into cracks in the river bank or bed, weakening rock until pieces break off — no sediment needed.
Hydraulic action is when rocks in the river smash into each other.

mcqs.q: Why has the Richter scale been largely replaced by the moment magnitude scale?
options: The Richter scale is still the standard scale used by all seismologists.
Moment magnitude measures damage while Richter measures shaking.
Deltas form in cold climates and estuaries in warm climates.
Richter saturates above magnitude ~7 and was calibrated for local Californian quakes; moment magnitude (Mw) measures the total energy released and works for all sizes globally.

mcqs.q: Why do some rivers form deltas and others form estuaries?
options: Deltas form in cold climates and estuaries in warm climates.
Deltas form where rivers deposit sediment faster than the sea can remove it (calm seas, heavy load); estuaries form where tidal energy removes sediment (strong tides).
Moment magnitude measures damage while Richter measures shaking.
Deltas form on big rivers and estuaries on small ones.
